opus-5.5.text:
I think it shows up more in the framing than in any single technical detail. Sergey has this habit of starting from a picture of the future that sounds like science fiction, like a general-purpose robot that can walk into any home and just figure out how to fold your laundry or clean the kitchen, and then working backward to ask what the most direct path to get there is. A lot of people in robotics would say that's too ambitious and start with one narrow task in one lab. His instinct is the opposite: if you believe the sci-fi version is actually reachable, you should build toward generality from day one.

You can see that in how the papers are written. They're not just "we improved success rate on this benchmark by five points." They often say, here's a step toward a robot foundation model that can work across many embodiments and many tasks, and here's evidence the recipe scales. The motivation section reads almost like a vision statement.

There's also the more playful side. Sergey reads a lot and likes thinking about what intelligence looks like when it's embodied, what it means for a machine to learn from its own experience the way people do. That curiosity seeps into the research questions: open-world generalization, robots doing long, messy, real household tasks instead of clean tabletop demos, learning from mistakes in deployment. Those are exactly the scenarios science fiction imagines, and he takes them seriously as engineering targets.

So I wouldn't say there's a literal sci-fi reference hidden in the papers. It's more that the ambition and the choice of problems come from someone who genuinely thinks that future is coming, and wants to be the one who builds it rather than just writes about it.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it shows up less in the specific content of the papers and more in how he picks problems. Sergey has this instinct for asking "what would this look like if it actually worked, in the way a sci-fi reader imagines it working?" and then reverse-engineering from that image back to a research question we can actually test. A lot of robotics people start from what the hardware can do today and push forward incrementally. He tends to start from the end state, a robot that can walk into an unfamiliar kitchen and just handle things, and then ask what's the minimal missing piece between here and there.

You can see it in how Pi frames its work. The emphasis on generalist policies, on one model across many robot bodies, on language as the interface, those are all very "science fiction" ideas in the sense that they're about the robot as a general agent rather than a specialized tool. The papers themselves are careful and empirical, with lots of ablations and honest failure cases, but the framing of the problem is unapologetically ambitious. I think that comes directly from someone who grew up reading about robots that could do anything and never fully accepted that the field had to settle for less.

The other place it shows is in his taste for things that look a little crazy at first. Training on huge amounts of heterogeneous robot data, letting the model figure out the embodiment differences on its own, folding dexterous tasks like laundry into a single policy. Five years ago many people would have said that's a fantasy. He's comfortable sitting with the fantasy long enough to find the tractable version of it. That's a very sci-fi reader's temperament: you take the speculative premise seriously, and then you work out the details rigorously.
